title: Calibration without Ground Truth
claim: Correcting a miscalibrated predictor amounts to projecting it onto the set compatible with a calibrated reference, moving it closer to truth.
layout: 1 panel, 2-D coordinate plot, diagonal constraint line, arrow from red to green point
description: A single 2-D Cartesian plot with a light grid. The x-axis is labeled Group A (q1) and the y-axis Group B (q2), both running from 0 to 1.0. A thick blue diagonal line runs from (0,1) to (1,0) and is labeled 'Compatible: q1 + q2 = 1'. A red dot at (0.1, 0.7) is labeled 'Strong Model (Miscalibrated)' in red text. A dark gray arrow points from the red dot up and to the right to a green dot on the blue line at (0.2, 0.8). The green dot is labeled 'projection (0.2, 0.8)' in bold green. The eye goes first to the red point, then along the arrow to the green point sitting on the blue line. Color coding separates the original model, the constraint, and the corrected output.
caption: Projection onto the reference-compatible set: transformations induced by ground truth extensions under which the reference is calibrated. The red point is the primary predictor, and the blue line is the constraint imposed by the calibrated reference. Under the chosen Bregman geometry (here we use Brier loss so the projection is Euclidean), the green point is the compatible map closest to the primary predictor. The specific numbers are derived from [ref].
abstract: We propose a label-free post-processing framework that improves a strong but miscalibrated primary model using a weaker yet better-calibrated reference. Our key insight is that strict worst-case improvement is possible if and only if the two models are not mutually calibrated, meaning there does not exist a joint distribution over their reports and outcomes such that both predictions are simultaneously calibrated. We formalize this condition and connect it to no-arbitrage results from economics. Under this condition, we develop an efficient post-processing algorithm for the strong model's outputs based on Bregman projection, with a strict worst-case performance improvement guarantee. Experiments on three 8B LLM families across three multiple-choice benchmarks show that our method reduces the primary model's ECE by over $40\%$ on common benchmarks.
